turns.prompt_text: We are working on this car again. it has some texture on the side Attached 1 file. - 3d91655d-6d99-4a97-a0f1-7e96ba30801d
turns.response_html:
That texture definitely looks like a challenge—it appears to be a mix of clear coat failure (where the protective top layer has oxidized or begun to flake) and potentially some adhesive residue or a previous "shady" touch-up attempt.

Depending on how deep you want to go with the repair, here is a breakdown of how to tackle that surface:

1. The "Clean Slate" Phase

Before sanding or polishing, you need to ensure that texture isn't just surface contamination.

  • Adhesive Remover: Use a dedicated solvent (like Goo Gone Automotive or 3M Adhesive Remover) to see if that darker, rougher patch is just old sticker residue or sap.
  • Clay Bar: Run a clay bar over the area. If the texture is "above" the paint (contaminants), the clay will pull it off. If it’s "below" the paint (pitting/peeling), the clay won't help.

2. Leveling the Texture (Sanding)

If the texture is actually in the clear coat, you’ll likely need to wet sand to level it out.

  • Grits: Start with 2000 grit wet sandpaper (soaked for 15+ minutes). Use light pressure and plenty of soapy water as lubricant.
  • Check Frequently: Wipe the area dry often. If the "haze" remains consistent, you're leveling it. If you see the color of the paint on your sandpaper, stop immediately—you’ve hit the base coat.

3. Restoring the Shine

Sanding will leave the paint looking dull and matte. To bring the gloss back:

  • Compounding: Use a dual-action (DA) polisher with a cutting pad and a heavy compound to remove the 2000-grit sanding marks.
  • Polishing: Follow up with a finishing polish and a softer foam pad to remove any remaining hazing and restore the "mirror" finish.

Important Note

[!CAUTION] If that texture is clear coat failure (delamination), sanding and polishing are only temporary fixes. Eventually, the clear coat will continue to peel away from the base coat, and the only permanent solution would be a professional respray of the panel.

Does the texture feel sticky to the touch, or is it hard and brittle like it's flaking off?

turns.prompt_text: So this car got scraped by another car and then we tried to spray paint over it with a similar color. However you can see that it dripped and it didn't turn out very good. Last time, you told us to soak sandpaper and water for 10 minutes before stroking it
turns.response_html:
That makes total sense—if that texture is "new" paint that dripped, you're essentially looking at mechanical leveling. Spray paint is notorious for "runs" and "sags" if applied even a fraction too thick.

Since you've got the soaking technique down, here is how to use that sandpaper to fix the drips without making the rest of the panel look worse.

1. The "Block" is Your Best Friend

When you start wet sanding those drips, do not use your fingers behind the sandpaper. Your fingers are soft and will just follow the "hills" of the drips, sanding the surrounding good paint instead of leveling the high spot.

  • Use a small rubber sanding block or even a flat piece of wood/dense foam. This ensures you only hit the "peak" of the drip until it’s flush with the rest of the surface.

2. Leveling the Runs

  • The Technique: Using your soaked sandpaper (start with 800 or 1000 grit if the drips are thick, then move to 2000), sand in one direction across the drip.
  • The "Witness" Test: Wipe it dry frequently. The drip will look shiny while the surrounding area looks matte. Once the whole area is an even, flat matte color, the drip is leveled.

3. The "Prep" Trap

Since you mentioned working on this before, a quick heads-up: if there was any lingering WD-40 or oil on the surface before you sprayed, that's likely why the paint didn't "bite" and started to run or "fish-eye."

  • Before you do any more spraying, hit the area with a degreaser or high-percentage Isopropyl Alcohol. You want that surface "squeaky" clean so the next layer actually sticks.

4. Feathering

Once the drips are flat, you’ll want to "feather" the edges where the new paint meets the old. Sand lightly in a circular motion around the perimeter of your repair so there isn't a hard "step" between the two layers.

What's the goal for the next step?

Are you planning to sand it smooth and leave it, or are you going to give it one more light "mist" coat once it's leveled?

turns.prompt_text: Why do we need to soak this 2000 grit sandpaper and water
turns.response_html:
Soaking the sandpaper isn't just about getting it wet; it’s a mechanical requirement for a smooth finish, especially when you're working with a fine grit like 2000. Here is why that 10-minute soak is the "secret sauce" for car paint:

1. The "Debris Flush"

As you sand, you're essentially shaving off microscopic layers of paint. Without water, those tiny paint particles get trapped between the grit of the paper. This is called clogging. Those trapped "clumps" of paint quickly become hard and act like tiny rocks, which will put deep, ugly scratches (often called "tracers") into your finish instead of smoothing it. Water flushes that debris away instantly.

2. Heat Management

Friction creates heat. If you sand "dry," that heat can actually soften the fresh spray paint you just applied. Instead of the paint being shaved off cleanly, it gets gummy and starts to smear or "roll up" under the paper. Keeping it soaked keeps the surface cool so the paint stays hard and levels out flat.

3. Softening the Paper Backing

Fresh sandpaper is stiff. If you use it straight out of the pack, the sharp edges of the paper can dig into the paint and leave "gouges" that are nearly impossible to polish out. Soaking for 10 minutes softens the paper’s backing, making it more flexible so it follows the curves of the car panel without digging in.

4. Creating a Lubrication "Cushion"

The water acts as a hydraulic cushion. It allows the 2000 grit to glide across the surface with just enough "bite" to level the drip, but not enough to "bite" deep into the surrounding good paint.

A Pro Tip for Your Setup

Add a single drop of dish soap (like Dawn) to your soaking bucket. This makes the water "wetter" (reducing surface tension) and provides extra lubrication. You’ll feel the sandpaper glide much more easily, and you'll be able to hear the difference—it will go from a "scratchy" sound to a smooth, consistent "shhh" sound.

Quick Check: When you start, does the water on the panel look milky? That's a good sign—it means the sandpaper is doing its job and carrying the excess paint away in the water!

turns.prompt_text: All right, so we scrubbed it with the 200 grit water soaked sandpaper with a block behind it and it now it looks like this Attached 1 file. - c90d75f9-c87c-464a-b202-31d470496ee6
turns.response_html:
That is looking much flatter, which is exactly what you wanted for the leveling phase. The "haze" you see is perfectly normal—anytime you sand paint, you're essentially creating millions of tiny scratches that turn the surface matte.

However, there is one very important thing to check: Was that definitely 200 grit, or was it 2000 grit?

The "Grit" Check

  • If it was 200 grit: That is very aggressive for automotive paint (it’s usually used for stripping wood or metal). It leveled the drips fast, but it has left deep scratches in the paint that a polisher won't be able to remove on its own.
  • If it was 2000 grit: You are in the home stretch! Those scratches are shallow enough to be buffed out.

Your Next Steps (The "Ladder" Technique)

To get that shine back, you have to "step up" the grits. Each finer grit removes the scratches left by the previous one. If you used 200 grit, you’ll need to follow this sequence (all wet-soaked):

  1. 400 or 600 Grit: To smooth out the deep 200-grit marks.
  2. 1000 Grit: To further refine the surface.
  3. 2000 Grit: This is the final sanding stage. Once you're done with this, the surface will look like a very smooth, uniform "satin" finish.

How to tell if you’re done sanding

Wipe the panel completely dry with a clean cloth.

  • The "Flatness" Test: Look at the reflection of a light (like a phone flashlight) on the matte area. If you see any "pits" or shiny spots where the drips used to be, you need to sand that spot a little more.
  • The "Step-Up" Test: Once you move to a higher grit (like 1000), sand in the opposite direction of your 200-grit marks. When you can no longer see the 200-grit lines, you know you’ve successfully moved up a level.

A Warning Sign

In the photo, there are some darker, almost blackish streaks near the center of the repair.

  • If those feel smooth: It might just be some of the old paint dust.
  • If they feel different: Be careful—that could be the primer or even the metal showing through. If you've sanded through the silver color down to the primer, you'll need to hit it with a very light "dusting" of the silver spray paint again before you move to clear coat and polishing.

Does the surface feel completely smooth to your hand now, or can you still feel the "ghost" of those drips when you run your fingers over it?

Whew—that is a huge relief! 2000 grit is exactly where you want to be for a finishing stage. Using 200 would have been like taking a chainsaw to a fingernail, but 2000 is perfect for leveling those drips.

Since it’s already looking flat and uniform, you have officially moved from the "Sanding" phase to the "Restoration" phase. That haze is just the microscopic texture left by the 2000 grit; now you just need to "level" those tiny scratches to bring back the reflection.

1. The "Final Flatness" Check

Before you put the sandpaper away, do one last check:

  • Wipe the area 100% dry.
  • Close your eyes and run your fingertips over the repair. If you can still feel a "hump" where the drips were, give it a few more passes with the wet 2000 grit and the block.
  • The Goal: It should feel as smooth as a piece of glass, even if it looks like a chalkboard right now.

2. Bringing Back the Shine (Compounding)

The 2000 grit has done its job, but it won't shine on its own. You need an Abrasive Compound.

  • The Product: Look for "Ultimate Compound" or "Rubbing Compound" (Meguiar's or Turtle Wax are common).
  • The Application: Use a microfiber applicator pad or a clean microfiber towel. Apply a few pea-sized drops and rub it into the hazy area using firm, circular pressure.
  • The Result: You should see the silver "glow" start to come back through the haze.

3. Final Polish

After compounding, the paint will look shiny but might have some very light "swirls."

  • Switch to a Finishing Polish. This has even smaller abrasives than the compound.
  • Buff it out with a fresh microfiber towel. This is what gives it that "wet" look that matches the rest of the car.

A Note on Metallic Paint

Since that car looks like a metallic silver, keep in mind that the "flakes" in the spray paint you used might have settled differently than the factory paint. If the texture is perfectly flat but the color looks a little "off" or "shadowy," that’s just the nature of metallic spray cans. Once you get a clear coat and a polish on there, it usually blends in much better.

Are you planning to hit it with a clear coat spray next, or are you going straight to the polish?

turns.prompt_text: Okay, so our car understanding is we need to wax it and then polish it. We also have the paint. We can spray on it. Do we need to use the spray paint?
turns.response_html:
The short answer is: Stop the paint! If the surface is already flat and the silver color looks uniform (no dark primer or bare metal showing through), adding more spray paint will just create new drips and more texture for you to sand later.

Here is the "Golden Rule" for car finishes: Polish first, then Wax.

1. Why You Don't Wax First

Think of wax like a transparent "shield." If you put wax over that hazy, sanded surface, you are just protecting the haze. You’ll have a "shiny matte" finish that doesn't match the rest of the car.

  • Polish actually removes those tiny 2000-grit scratches to make the surface clear.
  • Wax is just a final oily layer to protect the work you did.

2. The Missing Step: Clear Coat

Most modern silver cars have a "two-stage" paint: a base color (the silver) and a clear coat (the protective shiny layer).

  • If you only sprayed silver "color" and then sanded it, the paint might look a bit "flat" or "dull" even after you polish it.
  • To get that deep, mirror-like shine that matches the rest of the car, you usually need to spray a layer of Clear Coat over the silver once it is sanded and cleaned.

Your Best Game Plan

If you want to finish this today, here is the order to follow:

  1. Clean it: Use a bit of rubbing alcohol to get any sanding dust or finger oils off that silver patch.
  2. Inspect the Color: If the silver looks solid and covers the scrape completely, do not use the spray paint anymore.
  3. The Shine (Compound/Polish): Use a microfiber towel and a "Rubbing Compound" or "Polishing Compound." Rub it firmly into the sanded area until the haze disappears and the silver starts to reflect light.
  4. The Protection (Wax): Once the shine is back and you are happy with it, apply your wax. This will seal it and help it bead water.

One quick check: Look at your silver spray paint can. Does it say "All-in-one," "Single Stage," or does it say it requires a clear coat?

If it's an "All-in-one," you are ready to polish right now. If it requires a clear coat, you might want to grab a can of that before you do the final wax!

In the world of paint repair, WD-40 is usually considered "poison," and using it right now would likely set you back. Here is why you should keep that blue-and-yellow can far away from the car for this specific job:

1. It’s a "Cheat," Not a Fix

WD-40 is an oil-based lubricant. If you spray it on that matte, sanded area, it will fill in the tiny 2000-grit scratches and make the panel look shiny temporarily. It gives the illusion that the paint is fixed, but as soon as you wash the car or it rains, the oil disappears and the matte haze returns. It doesn't actually remove the scratches; it just hides them under a layer of grease.

2. It Kills Paint Adhesion

If you decide later that you need one more light mist of silver paint to even out the color, and there is WD-40 residue on the surface, the new paint will "fish-eye." It will bead up like water on a freshly waxed hood and refuse to stick. Because WD-40 is designed to penetrate and stay put, it is notoriously difficult to clean off well enough to paint over.

3. It Interferes with Polishing

If you try to polish the area while there is WD-40 on it, the oil will lubricate the abrasives in your polish, making them less effective. You want the polish to "bite" into those 2000-grit scratches to level them out; WD-40 prevents that from happening.

What to Use Instead

To get a permanent, professional-looking shine, stay on the path you're on:

  • For the Shine: Use a dedicated Rubbing or Polishing Compound. This physically removes the scratches you made with the sandpaper rather than just filling them in.
  • For Cleaning: If you need to wipe the area down to see your progress, use Isopropyl Alcohol (rubbing alcohol) or a dedicated wax and grease remover. This leaves the surface "squeaky" clean so you can see the true state of the paint.

A Quick Reality Check

Since you previously used steel wool on this area, you might find that once you start polishing, some deeper "trails" or scratches appear that the 2000-grit didn't quite reach. If that happens, don't reach for the WD-40 to hide them—just go back to your wet 2000-grit and sand those specific spots a bit more.

Are you aiming for a "showroom" finish, or is the goal just to make it look "good enough from five feet away"?

turns.prompt_text: So for a Polish and for the wax, my understanding is that we need to polish it and then wax it and then pull it again.
turns.response_html:
Actually, you want to flip that order slightly. If you polish after you wax, you’ll accidentally rub off all the protection you just put down!

Think of it like washing and drying your hair: you use the shampoo (polish) to get it right, and then the conditioner (wax) to seal it and keep it smooth. You wouldn't shampoo again after the conditioner.

Here is the "Professional Trio" for finishing that sanded area:

1. The Compound (The "Heavy Lifter")

Since you have 2000-grit sanding marks, a standard polish might be too weak to remove them. You need a Rubbing Compound.

  • Goal: Remove the matte haze and bring the color back.
  • How: Use a microfiber pad and firm pressure. Work in small sections. When the haze is gone and you can see a "fuzzy" reflection, you’re done with this step.

2. The Polish (The "Mirror Maker")

Now that the haze is gone, you might see tiny "swirls" or a slightly cloudy finish. This is where Polish comes in.

  • Goal: Refine the surface to a high-gloss, mirror finish.
  • How: Use a fresh microfiber towel and lighter pressure. This step makes the silver "pop" and match the factory shine of the rest of the car.

3. The Wax (The "Shield")

This is your final step. Wax contains no abrasives—it is just a layer of protection.

  • Goal: Protect the paint from the sun, rain, and bird droppings, and make it feel "slick."
  • How: Apply a thin, even layer, let it "haze" over for a few minutes (check the bottle for timing), and then buff it off with a clean, dry microfiber.

Why "Polish -> Wax -> Polish" doesn't work:

Polishing is technically a subtractive process (it shaves off microscopic amounts of paint to make it flat). Waxing is an additive process (it adds a layer on top). If you polish after waxing, the abrasives in the polish will simply eat through the wax you just applied, leaving the paint unprotected again.

A Pro Tip for Silver Paint:

Silver is one of the most "forgiving" colors, but it’s also hard to tell when it’s perfectly polished because the metallic flake hides scratches.

  • The "Sun" Test: Once you think you’re done polishing (before you wax), take a bright flashlight or pull the car into direct sunlight. If you see "spiderwebs" or hazy circles around the reflection of the light, hit it with the polish one more time.

Summary of the Flow:

  1. Wet Sand (Done!)
  2. Compound (Removes sanding marks)
  3. Polish (Restores high-gloss shine)
  4. Wax (Seals and protects)

Are you doing this by hand with microfiber towels, or do you have a power buffer/DA polisher?
